name: Mummia

lead: Mummia began as the name of a black, pitch-like bitumen used in Persian and Arab medicine for wounds and fractures. When European translators in the 12th century linked the word to Egyptian embalmed bodies, powdered mummy became a sought-after remedy.

Its appearance-related link is healing: it was used on bruises, wounds and bleeding, and in longevity-minded medicine as a panacea. The substance is now studied as a historical practice rather than used.

paras: Historically physicians prescribed mummia powder to be taken internally or applied to wounds. Artists also ground mummies into a brown oil pigment from the 17th to 19th centuries. A recent laboratory analysis of a historical sample reported an extract that modestly protected cells from flu-induced damage.
Historical mummia was often adulterated or made from recently dead bodies, and critics in the 16th century condemned the trade. Modern mummy-brown paint is made from minerals instead of remains.

angle.text: Physicians prescribed mummia for wounds, bruises and bleeding, and it was regarded as a general restorative. It is documented here as a historical remedy rather than a current appearance product.

lead: Mummia, also spelled mumia or mummy, was a group of substances used in medicine, ranging from a bitumen-like pitch to powdered human remains [1]. The name comes from the Arabic mumiya, a resinous bitumen used as medicine, which Greek writers rendered as pissasphaltus [1].

Persian physicians used the black pitch for wounds and fractures, and medieval Arab writers such as al-Razi and Ibn al-Baitar discussed it [1]. In the 12th century Europeans, with little access to natural bitumen, began to confuse it with the black residue from Egyptian mummies; traders then sold fake mummia, sometimes made from fresh corpses [1].

The remedy was valued as a cure-all and as an aphrodisiac. Sixteenth-century critics such as Pierre Belon and Ambroise Paré condemned the trade and its fraud, and by 1718 John Quincy wrote that it was largely out of prescription use, though Merck still listed it for sale in 1924 [1].

paras: Arab and Persian pharmacology described mumiya as a mountain pitch collected from rock seeps; Avicenna's Canon of Medicine is among the sources Grokipedia cites for it [2]. The Crusades spread European interest in the remedy [1].

Grokipedia reports that Gerard of Cremona misread Arabic texts in the 12th century and that Paracelsus later endorsed internal and topical use, while Paré applied it to battlefield wounds before abandoning it [2]. Wikipedia states Paré stopped prescribing it after condemning the trade [1].

A 2003 article in Medicina nei secoli describes the therapeutic compositions and uses of mummial remedies from the early modern period to the 18th century and notes that mummies were once seen as magical objects used as amulets [3]. Robert James's 1747 Pharmacopeia Universalis described mummy as resolving coagulated blood [2].
From the 17th to 19th centuries, artists ground mummies into the oil paint known as mummy brown; modern paints sold under that name use kaolin, quartz, goethite and hematite [1].

No studies found in humans. A recent laboratory analysis of Mumia vera aegyptiaca reportedly found that one extract modestly protected cells from influenza-induced damage, as summarized in a news aggregator post [4].
